guide.summary: Register a GitHub OAuth App in minutes: GitHub runs no app review, and the app can be used as soon as you have its client ID and client secret (organizations can still require owner approval under an OAuth app policy before it is authorized). Supports up to 10 callback URLs, 100 apps per owner, and standard OAuth2 with PKCE (S256 only; plain is not supported). 'Expire user access tokens' is enabled by default, giving 8-hour access tokens and refresh tokens that expire after 6 months without use. GitHub recommends GitHub Apps for finer-grained permissions.

difficulty.verdict: No GitHub app review; client ID/secret are available immediately after registration — note that organizations can still require owner approval via an OAuth app policy before members can authorize the app

time.verdict: No approval stage is documented; credentials are available right after registration

prerequisites.detail: Personal account, or an organization where you have administrative access — docs: you can register an OAuth app under your personal account or under any organization you have administrative access to
A publicly accessible URL for your application; docs warn to avoid sensitive data such as internal URLs in your OAuth app

At least one redirect URI (e.g., https://backend.composio.dev/api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback); up to 10 allowed. The redirect_uri your app sends must exactly match a registered callback URL unless wildcard matching is enabled (loopback addresses supported for local development)

steps.title: Sign in to GitHub
steps.action: Log in with the personal account or organization that will own the OAuth app
steps.nuances: If creating under an organization, you need administrative access to that org (docs: apps can be registered under your personal account or any organization you have administrative access to)

steps.title: Open Developer Settings → OAuth Apps
steps.action: Click profile picture → Settings → Developer settings → OAuth apps
steps.human_because: Navigation in GitHub UI requires human clicks
steps.nuances: Direct URL https://github.com/settings/developers works if already logged in

steps.title: Create new OAuth App
steps.action: Click "New OAuth App" (or "Register a new application" if first app)
steps.nuances: Owner can be your personal account or any organization where you have administrative access

steps.title: Fill required registration fields
steps.action: Enter Application name, Homepage URL, Authorization callback URL (add up to 10 via "Add callback URL"). Optionally add description, enable Device Flow (only if CLI/IoT/headless), and keep "Expire user access tokens" checked (default). Click "Register application".
steps.human_because: Form submission in provider console; legal acceptance of terms
steps.nuances: Docs do not impose a blanket HTTPS rule on callback URLs; avoid using sensitive data such as internal URLs in the app's information. Device Flow carries phishing risk if not needed; prefer authorization code with PKCE. "Expire user access tokens" is enabled by default: 8-hour access token, 6-month refresh token (lifetimes documented on the Authorizing OAuth apps page).

steps.title: Copy Client ID and generate Client Secret
steps.action: Copy the Client ID. Generate the Client Secret and copy it immediately (the UI displays it once — not stated in docs). Store both securely.
steps.human_because: Secret must be copied manually from the UI at generation time
steps.nuances: Every registered OAuth app is assigned a unique Client ID and Client Secret; never leak the secret and store it (e.g., environment variables or a key vault). If lost, generate a new one from the app settings (UI behavior — not documented). No app review — credentials work immediately.

steps.title: Configure scopes at authorization time
steps.action: When building the authorization URL, include desired scopes (e.g., repo, user, admin:org, offline_access). Scopes are not set during registration; users may grant fewer than requested.
steps.nuances: Roughly 35 scopes documented (including offline_access); overlapping scopes normalized (user + user:email → user). offline_access yields an expiring access token + refresh token even if the app is not configured for expiring tokens. Users may grant fewer scopes than requested — handle reduced access gracefully.

steps.title: Implement OAuth flow with PKCE and state
steps.action: Use authorization code grant with PKCE (code_challenge_method=S256; plain is not supported) and a random state parameter for CSRF protection. Exchange code for token within 10 minutes (code lifetime). Handle token refresh using refresh_token (if expiring tokens enabled); refresh rotates the token pair and scope cannot be changed on refresh.
steps.nuances: redirect_uri must exactly match a registered callback URL unless wildcard matching is enabled; loopback URLs may use a different port than the registered callback. Token limits: 2,000 access token requests/hour and ten tokens created per user/application/scope combination per hour (see Rate limits for OAuth apps page). SAML SSO: tokens do not access organizations where the user has not completed SSO; check GET /user/installations regularly (see Best practices page).

gotchas.title: Token request and sign-in rate limits
gotchas.why_it_matters: OAuth apps are limited to 2,000 access token requests per hour; if an app signs the user in ten times within one hour, the next sign-in within the same hour requires re-authorization. There is also a limit of ten tokens issued per user/application/scope combination and a rate limit of ten tokens created per hour.
gotchas.how_to_handle: Cache tokens, implement exponential backoff, and avoid redundant token exchanges

gotchas.title: REST API rate limit is the user's 5,000 requests/hour
gotchas.why_it_matters: OAuth app tokens use the authenticated user's rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour, shared with other requests made on the user's behalf — GitHub Apps instead get limits that scale with users/repositories.
gotchas.how_to_handle: Monitor the x-ratelimit-* response headers (the authoritative rate limit status), honor x-ratelimit-reset before retrying, and back off on 403/429 responses

gotchas.title: Token expiration default (8h access, 6-month refresh)
gotchas.why_it_matters: With "Expire user access tokens" enabled (the default), the access token expires after 8 hours and the refresh token expires after 6 months without use; refresh rotates the pair (old access and refresh tokens stop working) and scope cannot be changed on refresh. Docs frame unchecking the option for apps not yet updated to support short-lived tokens; requesting the offline_access scope yields expiring tokens even when the app-level setting is off.
gotchas.how_to_handle: Implement refresh token flow; store refresh tokens securely (separately from access tokens); handle 401 by refreshing

gotchas.title: 100 OAuth apps per owner limit
gotchas.why_it_matters: A single user or organization cannot own more than 100 OAuth apps
gotchas.how_to_handle: Audit existing apps; delete unused ones; consider GitHub Apps for new integrations

gotchas.title: Maximum 10 callback URLs per app
gotchas.why_it_matters: Cannot add more than 10 redirect URIs; wildcard matching should only be enabled when necessary because it lets an attacker send authorization codes
gotchas.how_to_handle: Plan all environments (dev, staging, prod) upfront; use path-based differentiation

gotchas.title: Device Flow phishing risk
gotchas.why_it_matters: Enabling Device Flow without need exposes phishing risk; the device flow needs no redirect URIs, so an attacker can remotely impersonate your app. Prefer authorization code with PKCE.
gotchas.how_to_handle: Leave unchecked unless building a device-authorization-grant flow

gotchas.title: SAML SSO restrictions
gotchas.why_it_matters: If an organization uses SAML SSO and the user has not performed SAML SSO, the user access token will not have access to that organization
gotchas.how_to_handle: Regularly check the GET /user/installations endpoint to verify which organizations a token can access; guide users to complete SSO for target orgs

gotchas.title: Organization OAuth app policies can gate usage
gotchas.why_it_matters: There is no GitHub-run review of OAuth apps, but organizations can restrict them: when an organization application policy is active, a member's request to install an OAuth app must be approved or denied by an organization owner before it can be used.
gotchas.how_to_handle: Before rolling out inside an organization, check its OAuth app policy and have an owner approve the app

gotchas.title: GitHub Apps preferred for new integrations
gotchas.why_it_matters: GitHub Apps offer fine-grained permissions, repository-level install, short-lived tokens (installation tokens expire after about 1 hour), and rate limits that scale with users/repositories; OAuth apps can only act as the authenticated user and use the user's 5,000 requests/hour limit
gotchas.how_to_handle: Evaluate GitHub App instead if you need repo-scoped access, higher limits, or organization-level installation

agent_can: Draft OAuth app manifest (name, homepage, callback URLs, description)
Prepare authorization URL with PKCE parameters and state
Implement token exchange and refresh logic
Monitor rate limit headers and handle backoff
human_must: Navigate to Developer Settings and click "New OAuth App"
Fill and submit the registration form
Copy Client ID and generate/copy Client Secret at generation time
Complete SAML SSO for target organizations (tokens only access orgs where SSO is done)

sources.title: Creating an OAuth app
sources.what_it_supports: Registration steps and navigation, required/optional form fields, "Enable Device Flow" checkbox, "Expire user access tokens" enabled by default, up to 10 callback URLs, up to 100 OAuth apps per user/organization, registration under personal account or organization with administrative access, avoid sensitive/internal URLs warning

sources.title: Building OAuth apps (overview)
sources.what_it_supports: OAuth apps act on behalf of a user; scopes limit token access; GitHub Apps preferred for fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens. Does not document any review process either way

sources.title: Authorizing OAuth apps
sources.what_it_supports: Authorization URL and parameters (client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state), PKCE S256 (plain unsupported), 10-minute authorization code lifetime, POST /login/oauth/access_token, refresh_token grant and rotation, 8-hour access token / 6-month refresh token, offline_access scope, ten tokens per user/application/scope combination and ten created per hour, redirect_uri exact-match rule and loopback port exception

sources.title: Scopes for OAuth apps
sources.what_it_supports: Scope list (~35 including offline_access), scope normalization (user + user:email → user), users may grant fewer scopes than requested, offline_access behavior

sources.title: Rate limits for OAuth apps
sources.what_it_supports: 2,000 access token requests/hour, 10 sign-ins per user/hour then re-authorization required, secondary rate limits, GitHub Apps limits scale while OAuth app limits are lower

sources.title: Best practices for creating an OAuth app
sources.what_it_supports: Wildcard callbacks only when necessary, device flow phishing risk, 8-hour/6-month token lifetimes, secure storage of client secret and tokens, SAML SSO check via GET /user/installations, GitHub Apps preferred

sources.title: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps
sources.what_it_supports: Granular permissions vs scopes, repository-level installation, ~1-hour installation tokens, OAuth apps use the user's 5,000 requests/hour limit, organization owner approval of OAuth app installs under org application policy

sources.title: Rate limits for the REST API
sources.what_it_supports: 5,000 requests/hour personal rate limit for user access tokens, x-ratelimit-* headers as authoritative status, 5,000 requests/hour per OAuth app when fetching public data with client ID/secret

sources.title: Authenticating to the REST API with an OAuth app
sources.what_it_supports: Every registered OAuth app is assigned a unique Client ID and Client Secret; do not leak the secret; store as environment variables

unverified: Exact Composio integration behavior for GitHub OAuth (snippet not verifiable from GitHub docs)
Whether GitHub enforces any unpublished limits beyond documented ones
Whether the OAuth app client secret can be viewed again after generation (docs never state 'shown only once'; that is UI behavior)
Whether non-loopback plain-HTTP callback URLs are accepted (docs state no blanket HTTPS requirement — only the loopback port exception for redirect_uri matching is documented)

An explicit official statement that OAuth apps undergo no review/approval (no OAuth docs page mentions a review process; organization-level OAuth app policies can still require owner approval before use)
